body:
The emergence of planned cities

The Harappan Civilisation, also called the Indus Civilisation, was one of the earliest urban civilisations of the Indian subcontinent. Its mature urban phase is generally dated to approximately 2600–1900 BCE. Important cities included Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi.

The most distinctive feature of these settlements was their planned urban organisation. Streets, houses, drains, wells, platforms and large buildings were arranged according to recognisable patterns. At major centres such as Mohenjodaro, the relationship between streets, buildings and drainage indicates that important parts of the settlement were planned before individual houses were constructed.

Urban planning means arranging the different parts of a settlement to meet the needs of its inhabitants. In Harappan cities, this included providing routes for movement, places for residence and collective activities, access to water, facilities for removing wastewater and substantial walls around important areas.

Urban planning

Urban planning is the organised arrangement of streets, buildings, residential areas, public facilities and essential infrastructure within a town or city.

The Citadel and the Lower Town

Many major Harappan settlements contained two distinguishable sections. The relatively small, elevated section is called the Citadel, while the more extensive, lower section is called the Lower Town.

At Mohenjodaro, the Citadel stood on a massive mud-brick platform and was separated from the Lower Town by substantial walls. The Lower Town contained extensive residential neighbourhoods and was also protected by walls.

FeatureCitadelLower Town
Relative positionGenerally higherGenerally lower
Relative extentUsually smallerUsually larger
Location in the common arrangementWestern sectionEastern section
Characteristic structuresLarge platforms and distinctive buildingsResidential houses, streets, wells and drains
ExampleGreat Bath at MohenjodaroCourtyard houses at Mohenjodaro

Why was the elevated section important?

Raising buildings on substantial platforms created an elevated area that was physically distinct from surrounding neighbourhoods. Such platforms also provided strong foundations for large structures. At some settlements, elevation and massive walls may additionally have helped protect buildings from flooding or regulate access.

The Citadel contained buildings that appear to have served special or collective purposes. However, Citadel does not automatically mean royal palace. The precise political organisation of Harappan cities is not established, and the functions of several major buildings remain uncertain.

The Lower Town was not an unplanned settlement outside the main city. At Mohenjodaro, its streets, houses, bathrooms and drains demonstrate a high degree of planning.

Not every city followed exactly the same arrangement

The division into a higher Citadel and a lower residential section is a useful general model, but it was not an identical blueprint followed everywhere. Dholavira in Gujarat had 3 broad urban divisions, including a fortified central complex, a Middle Town and a Lower Town. Lothal had a raised upper section that was not separately enclosed by its own wall, although the settlement had wider fortifications.

Harappan cities shared important planning principles, but their internal divisions, construction materials, water systems and public buildings varied from one settlement to another.

Prelims focus

  • The Mature Harappan urban phase is generally dated to approximately 2600–1900 BCE.
  • The typical Citadel was smaller and higher; the Lower Town was larger and lower.
  • In the common arrangement, the Citadel occupied the western section and the Lower Town the eastern section.
  • Mohenjodaro had large mud-brick platforms and substantial walls separating its principal sections.
  • Dholavira is an important exception to the simple 2-part model.
  • Trap: A Citadel is not necessarily a confirmed royal residence.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, pp. 32–34; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 1, 5–6; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation, pp. 90–92.]

title: The Harappan City: An Introduction to Planned Urban Settlements

body:
Streets arranged in a grid pattern

A major feature of Harappan town planning was the systematic arrangement of streets. At Mohenjodaro, the principal streets and smaller lanes followed an approximately rectangular or gridiron pattern.

In a gridiron plan, streets running broadly north–south intersect streets running broadly east–west, often at or near right angles. The intersections divide the settlement into blocks containing houses and other buildings.

Major streets provided routes through the settlement, while narrower lanes gave access to individual houses. The arrangement also helped create continuous routes for drainage channels.

Streets and drainage were planned together

The relationship between buildings and streets is particularly clear at Mohenjodaro. Many houses had bathing areas connected to drains running along streets. For wastewater to enter these street drains, houses needed suitable connections along their street-facing walls.

This suggests that the principal streets and drainage routes were laid out before, or in coordination with, the residential buildings. Planning therefore extended beyond straight roads to the arrangement of essential infrastructure.

Standardised bricks and construction

Harappan builders used both sun-dried mud bricks and baked bricks. Sun-dried bricks were suitable for many walls, platforms and foundations. Baked bricks, which were more resistant to moisture, were particularly valuable in structures exposed to water, including drains, bathing areas and wells.

One important indication of standardisation was the regular proportion of bricks used at many Harappan settlements.

Standard Harappan brick proportion

The commonly used proportion of thickness : width : length was approximately 1 : 2 : 4.

The same relationship can be expressed as length : width : thickness = 4 : 2 : 1.

Thus, if a brick had a thickness of 10 cm, the corresponding standard proportion would give a width of 20 cm and a length of 40 cm. These dimensions illustrate the proportion; they were not the dimensions of every Harappan brick.

At many settlements, bricks were arranged in an interlocking pattern, with successive courses placed so that joints did not form continuous vertical lines. This improved the stability and strength of masonry walls.

The use of standard proportions across widely separated settlements indicates shared construction practices. It does not mean that every building had identical dimensions or materials.

Platforms and raised foundations

Large Harappan structures were often erected on raised mud-brick platforms. At Mohenjodaro, extensive platforms formed the foundation of the elevated Citadel and supported major structures.

Building on raised foundations helped establish stable construction levels and could also help protect structures from water accumulation. Once these platforms were established, they influenced the placement of subsequent buildings.

Fortifications and enclosed areas

Fortifications were substantial walls enclosing settlements or important sections within them. Harappan fortifications were commonly constructed using mud bricks, sometimes with baked-brick facing or stone masonry.

Walls could serve several purposes:

  • Protection: Providing a physical barrier around a settlement or important area.
  • Controlled access: Directing movement through designated gateways.
  • Separation: Marking boundaries between different sections of a settlement.
  • Environmental protection: In some locations, substantial walls and platforms could help reduce damage from flooding.

Fortifications should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of frequent warfare. Their functions could differ according to the needs and location of each settlement.

Construction materials also varied regionally. At Dholavira, local stone was extensively used alongside mud bricks. This contrasts with the particularly prominent baked-brick construction at Mohenjodaro.

Prelims focus

  • Mohenjodaro had an approximately gridiron street pattern.
  • Major streets commonly intersected at approximately right angles.
  • Standard Harappan brick proportions were approximately 1 : 2 : 4 in thickness, width and length.
  • Sun-dried and baked bricks were both used in Harappan construction.
  • Fortifications and raised platforms were important features of major settlements.
  • Trap: Fortifications do not establish that every Harappan city was primarily a military settlement.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 5–7; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, pp. 33–34; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, pp. 91–92; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Outstanding Universal Value, Criterion (iv), consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Streets, Building Materials and Fortifications in Harappan Cities

body:
Residential architecture in the Lower Town

The houses excavated at Mohenjodaro provide important evidence of Harappan domestic architecture. Many were constructed around a central courtyard, with rooms opening onto it from different sides.

The courtyard probably served as an important space for everyday household activities, including cooking, weaving and other domestic work. In a hot climate, an open courtyard could provide light and air while allowing activities to take place within the privacy of the house.

Houses varied considerably in size. Some were relatively modest, while others contained numerous rooms, courtyards and additional facilities. However, different house sizes did not prevent builders from using broadly similar construction techniques.

A representative courtyard house

A substantial Harappan house could contain several connected spaces:

  • Entrance: A doorway opening from a street or lane, often arranged so that the interior courtyard was not directly visible from outside.
  • Courtyard: An open internal space surrounded by rooms.
  • Rooms: Enclosed spaces used for domestic activities and storage.
  • Bathroom: An area commonly paved with bricks and connected to a wastewater outlet.
  • Staircase: Present in some houses, providing access to an upper storey or roof.
  • Well: Present in some houses and sometimes accessible from outside the house.

Privacy in house design

The arrangement of entrances and windows suggests that privacy was important in some Harappan residential buildings.

At Mohenjodaro, many houses had no windows opening directly onto the street at ground level. In addition, entrances were often positioned so that someone standing outside could not look directly into the central courtyard.

These architectural features provided separation between the public street and private household activities. They do not establish that every Harappan family followed identical social customs.

Bathrooms and domestic drainage

Bathing areas were a particularly notable feature of Harappan houses. At Mohenjodaro, excavated houses commonly had brick-paved bathrooms with wastewater outlets leading through walls towards street drains.

Water used for bathing or cleaning could therefore be carried away without flowing across the main living areas or accumulating inside the house.

This connection between domestic architecture and public drainage shows that sanitation was incorporated into the residential plan.

Upper storeys and wells

The remains of staircases in several houses indicate that some buildings had an upper storey or accessible roof. Although the upper portions of these buildings have generally disappeared, their ground-floor staircases show that not all residential structures were single-storeyed.

Some houses contained wells made from carefully arranged bricks. In certain cases, a well was located in a room that could also be approached from outside, suggesting that people beyond the household may have had access to its water.

A house was more than a group of rooms

In a well-planned Harappan neighbourhood, houses were connected to the surrounding city through entrances, streets, water facilities and wastewater outlets.

Prelims focus

  • Many Mohenjodaro houses had rooms arranged around a courtyard.
  • Brick-paved bathing areas were common in residential buildings.
  • Some houses had staircases indicating upper storeys or roof access.
  • Some houses contained wells, occasionally accessible from outside.
  • House entrances often prevented a direct view into the courtyard.
  • Trap: Not every Harappan house was identical in size, height or facilities.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, Section 3.2, Domestic architecture, p. 7; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, p. 34.]

title: Harappan Houses: Courtyards, Bathrooms and Residential Neighbourhoods

body:
Why drainage was necessary

A densely populated settlement produces wastewater from bathing, cleaning, washing and other household activities. Unless this water is removed, it can collect in living spaces and streets.

Many Harappan towns addressed this problem through carefully constructed drainage systems. Mohenjodaro provides one of the clearest examples of an organised network connecting household drains with larger street drains.

The movement of wastewater

In a typical Mohenjodaro drainage arrangement, wastewater followed a connected route from the house towards the street.

  1. Bathing area: Used water collected at a paved bathing area or household outlet.
  2. House drain: A channel carried the water through or alongside the building wall.
  3. Sump or cesspit: In many installations, the water first entered a pit where heavier solid matter could settle.
  4. Street drain: Water passed into a larger channel constructed along the street.
  5. Further disposal: The drainage route carried the wastewater away from the immediate household area.

Construction of street drains

Street drains were often constructed with baked bricks set in mortar. They were designed with a gentle downward slope, allowing wastewater to move through the channel under the influence of gravity.

The drains were commonly covered with bricks or stone slabs. Covering helped protect the channels and allowed the surrounding areas to remain usable.

Several features made the system particularly practical:

  • Connected channels: Smaller household drains could discharge into larger street drains.
  • Sloping surfaces: A gentle gradient helped water flow rather than remain stagnant.
  • Removable covers: Bricks or slabs could be lifted to expose the channels.
  • Inspection and cleaning points: Access openings and sumps allowed accumulated material to be removed.
  • Settling pits: Solid waste could collect in a sump before wastewater passed onward.

Maintenance was part of the design

Even a well-constructed drain can become blocked when sand, mud and other materials accumulate. Harappan builders therefore provided access for cleaning.

The presence of removable covers and cleaning points shows that the system was not merely a channel for water. It was designed to remain serviceable over time.

This is an important distinction between a simple open gutter and an organised network of covered, maintainable drains.

Drainage was not identical at every settlement

Although an elaborate street-drain network is characteristic of Mohenjodaro, it should not be assumed that every Harappan town possessed the same system.

At Lothal, drains made with baked bricks were found even though many houses were built with mud bricks. This shows that builders could choose different materials for residential walls and water-carrying structures.

At Kalibangan in Rajasthan, the excavated Lower Town followed a planned street pattern, but a regular network of continuous street drains was not identified. Household drains made from wood or baked bricks commonly discharged into soakage jars buried in the streets. This illustrates a different method of disposing of household wastewater.

Urban planning and drainage are related but not identical

A settlement may have straight, regularly arranged streets without possessing the same continuous drainage network found at Mohenjodaro. The correct description depends on the particular site.

Prelims focus

  • Mohenjodaro is especially known for its organised, covered drainage network.
  • House drains commonly connected with larger street drains.
  • Gentle slopes helped wastewater flow through the channels.
  • Removable covers, inspection openings and sumps facilitated cleaning.
  • Kalibangan used household drains and soakage jars rather than a regular continuous street-drain network.
  • Trap: A grid-pattern town does not necessarily have a Mohenjodaro-type drainage system.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, p. 34; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 1, Sections 3.1–3.2, pp. 6–7; Archaeological Survey of India, Excavations at Kalibangan: The Harappans (1960–69), Part I, 2015, Chapter 6, KLB-2 Stratigraphy and Structures, p. 146.]

title: The Harappan Drainage System and Urban Sanitation
